numberItems.stem: Around which hazard classes must you never smoke while loading or unloading?
options: Class 1, Division 2.1, Class 3, Class 4 and Class 5
numberItems.explanation: Never smoke around 5 classes: Class 1, Division 2.1, Class 3, Class 4 and Class 5. The cargo heater list (1, 2.1, 3) is shorter (p. 9-11).

numberItems.stem: How many hazard classes do the cargo heater rules cover?
numberItems.explanation: Cargo heater rules cover 3: Class 1, Division 2.1 and Class 3, and they include heater/air-conditioner units (p. 9-12).

numberItems.stem: Which hazard classes may NOT be carried as overhang or tailgate loads (unless every package is fire- and water-resistant or tarped)?
numberItems.explanation: Class 1, Class 4 and Class 5 need a closed cargo space unless all packages are fire- and water-resistant or covered by such a tarp (p. 9-12).

numberItems.stem: You haul Division 1.1 explosives in a combination vehicle. What may the other vehicle in the combination NOT carry?
numberItems.explanation: Division 1.1 or 1.2 may not ride in a combination with a placarded cargo tank, or where the other vehicle carries 1.1 A, Class 7 Yellow III, 2.3 or 6.1, or a DOT Spec 106A or 110A tank (p. 9-12).

numberItems.stem: Corrosive liquids must NEVER be loaded next to or above which of these?
numberItems.explanation: Never load corrosive liquids next to or above Div. 1.4, 4.1, 4.3, Class 5 or Div. 2.3 Zone B (p. 9-13).

numberItems.stem: In the handbook's example, a radioactive package with a transport index of 1.1 may not be left within what distance of people or cargo-space walls?
numberItems.explanation: A package with a transport index of 1.1 can't be left within 2 feet of people or cargo-space walls (pp. 9-13, 9-22).

numberItems.stem: Using the radioactive separation table, how far from people or partitions must packages with a total transport index of 30.1–40.0 be?
numberItems.explanation: For a total transport index of 30.1–40.0, the table gives 6 ft to people or cargo compartment partitions; 11 ft is that row's distance to film for 2–4 hours (p. 9-22).

numberItems.stem: For a solid material, bulk packaging means a container holding:
options: A water capacity of more than 1,000 lb
More than 882 lb and more than 119 gallons
numberItems.explanation: For solids, bulk packaging holds more than 882 lb and more than 119 gallons. 1,000 lb water capacity is the gas rule; 64 cubic feet is a freight container (p. 9-24).

numberItems.stem: For a gas, bulk packaging means a container with:
options: A water capacity of more than 1,000 lb
A capacity of more than 882 lb
A capacity of 64 cubic feet or more
numberItems.explanation: For gases, bulk packaging has a water capacity of more than 1,000 lb (p. 9-24).

numberItems.stem: What are the most common cargo tanks for liquids and for gases?
options: MC331 for liquids, MC306 for gases
DOT Spec 106A for liquids, 110A for gases
MC306 for liquids, MC331 for gases
numberItems.explanation: The most common cargo tanks are the MC306 for liquids and the MC331 for gases (p. 9-15).

numberItems.stem: Where do you look up the ID number to show on a cargo tank or portable tank?
options: Column 7 of the Hazardous Materials Table
Column 4 of the Hazardous Materials Table
numberItems.explanation: Look up the ID number in Column 4 of the Hazardous Materials Table (p. 9-15).

numberItems.stem: A portable tank holds more than 1,000 gallons. How tall must the shipping-name letters be?
numberItems.explanation: Portable tanks over 1,000 gallons need shipping-name letters at least 2 inches tall on 2 opposite sides; under 1,000 gallons, 1 inch (p. 9-15).

numberItems.stem: A portable tank holds less than 1,000 gallons. Where must its ID number appear?
options: On each side and each end
numberItems.explanation: Under 1,000 gallons, the ID number goes on 2 opposite sides; at 1,000 gallons or more, on each side and each end (p. 9-15).

numberItems.stem: A freight container is a reusable container of at least what size?
numberItems.explanation: A freight container is a reusable container of 64 cubic feet or more that can be lifted with its contents inside (p. 9-24).
